One-sentence judgment: coil winders, tapers, and finishers do not just wind wire on, but operate or tend winding machines to wind wire into coils used in electrical components such as resistors and transformers and in electrical equipment and instruments such as field cores, forms, armature cores, motors, generators, and control devices, and they complete terminating, trimming, end treatment, insulation insertion, and inspection and testing; O*NET defines this occupation as "winding wire into coils for electrical components (such as resistors and transformers) and electrical equipment and instruments (such as field cores, forms, armature cores, motors, generators, and control devices)", and this page follows the exact occupation basis of O*NET-SOC 51-2021.00.

Signals for continued exploration: you are willing to work beside a winding machine for long periods of fine, repeated operations to a cycle time while keeping an eye on wire gauge, turns, end condition, and electrical test results; O*NET work context shows 100% wear common protective or safety equipment every day, 92% consider being exact or highly accurate extremely important, 87% use hands continuously or almost continuously to handle and feel tools and workpieces, 83% perform repetitive motions continuously, 57% are exposed to contaminants every day, 53% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 41% may be exposed to minor burns, cuts, or bites every day, and 44% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others.

Conditions for pausing high investment first: you have not yet completed one full closed loop of reading the work order and specification, selecting and loading materials, winding, end and insulation treatment, inspection or electrical test, and recording, and you have not checked the local and enterprise authority requirements for equipment operation, electrical testing, maintenance, and hazardous energy isolation; this occupation's preparation level is Job Zone 1-2 (little or some preparation), SVP below 6.0, and the education distribution on the page shows 57% of respondents answering that a high school diploma or equivalent is required, 41% answering that a postsecondary certificate is required, and 2% answering below high school diploma (the page shows only these three bands); the occupation page does not mark Bright Outlook for this code, and this page does not infer personal hiring probability from that.

Education, training, certificates, and position authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1-2 (little or some preparation), SVP below 6.0; the national certification page for this occupation shows that no certifications were found, so this page lists no certification names; a training certificate does not equal authorization to work, and equipment operation, electrical testing, maintenance, and hazardous energy isolation authority should be based on the position description, enterprise training, and applicable safety rules; in the United States, the employer's machine guarding and hazardous energy control obligations are set by applicable occupational safety regulations (this page expresses them under the general framework of 1910.212 and 1910.147), and human factors and ergonomics improvements are expressed according to the recommendations of public occupational health bodies; this page describes tasks and boundaries based on O*NET and public sources and does not write any training as a legal qualification.

In one sentence: this is an occupation where "whether turns and wire gauge are accurate, whether end and insulation treatment is sound, and whether equipment guards and hazardous energy isolation hold" determine success more than personal hand speed; if you are willing to treat fine repeated operations as something that must be done steadily every day, it is worth serious consideration.

The work of coil winders, tapers, and finishers can be divided into three connected but independent work surfaces. The first is winding work and equipment tending: reviewing work orders and specifications to determine the required materials and the types of parts to be processed, operating or tending winding machines to wind coils for resistors and transformers and for electrical equipment such as forms, motors, and generators, selecting and loading materials such as workpieces, objects, and machine parts onto the winding equipment, adjusting the equipment and tending the run to a cycle time, and stopping the machine and using tools to remove the finished part. The second is end, insulation, and coating treatment: using hand tools to terminate, reconnect, and trim materials such as wire, insulation, and coils, using pliers and wire strippers to cut, strip, and bend the wire ends at the coil ends, using sheet insulation to line the slots and inserting the coils into the slots, and using hand tools to apply solution or varnish to wound electrical parts and bake them. The third is inspection and testing and maintenance records: using measuring devices to inspect and test wound electrical parts such as motors, armatures, and stators and recording the test results, using hand tools to disassemble and assemble motors and to repair and maintain electrical parts and machine parts, and recording production and operating data on the required forms.
Operate or tend winding machines to wind wire into coils for electrical components and electrical equipment, and complete end treatment, insulation, and inspection and testing

Safety first; guards must not be bypassed for hazardous operation on one's own, and for applicable internal maintenance or jam clearing, energy must first be controlled through procedure; electrical exposure, testing, and re-energization follow the actual qualification procedures, and workstation posture and persistent discomfort are escalated according to assessment. US 1910.212 requires appropriate machine guarding at the point of operation and at in-running and rotating parts, and hand tools cannot replace guarding; guards must not be removed or bypassed for hazardous operation on one's own, and maintenance disassembly follows the actual control procedure, and not all disassembly is treated as prohibited. US 1910.147 covers maintenance that could cause injury from unexpected startup or release of stored energy, with applicable conditions and exceptions for normal production; an authorized employee must have real duty training, and a title does not automatically authorize. Stored energy is eliminated, disconnected, restrained, or made safe, and isolation and de-energization are verified before work, not uniformly zero energy; a stop button is not isolation, and re-energization follows procedure with verification of equipment, personnel clearing, and notification, so an anomaly disappearing does not automatically grant re-energization authority. US 1910.333 applies to scenarios exposing electrical hazards: in principle energy is disconnected first, and special conditions without de-energization must be verified by the employer and still carry safety procedures, so testing does not mean work may be performed energized at will. If de-energization was not locked or tagged through procedure, the circuit is still treated as energized, and a qualified person must verify that it cannot restart and use test equipment to confirm no voltage or backfeed or induced voltage; exposure to a circuit not de-energized is handled only by a qualified person with the required protection, and an ordinary winding title does not automatically confer qualification. Re-energization requires a qualified person to check tools and devices and clear and notify personnel through procedure, and it is not restored merely because measurements look normal.

Six recurring occupational judgments: whether winding parameters, wire gauge, and turns meet the specification; whether end stripping, bending, and insulation insertion are sound; whether electrical test and measurement results meet standard and are documented; whether equipment guards and hazardous energy isolation are in place; whether repetitive motion and awkward twisting postures are controlled; and whether production and test records are traceable.
Judgment one: whether winding parameters, wire gauge, and turns meet the specification

Check wire gauge, turns, tension, and layer arrangement against the work order, confirm the first article before batch winding, and stop the machine to adjust when a turn deviation or uneven layering appears rather than covering it up with later trimming.
Judgment two: whether end stripping, bending, and insulation insertion are sound

Handle the ends to the specified strip length and bend angle to avoid damaging the wire or leaving burrs; fit the insulation sheet and slot by process and do not force it in, which can crush the wire.
Judgment three: whether electrical test and measurement results meet standard and are documented

Complete measurement and electrical testing to procedure and record the results; when a deviation or insulation anomaly appears, isolate the item first and report it rather than writing the test record as a pass.
Judgment four: whether equipment guards and hazardous energy isolation are in place

US 1910.147 covers maintenance that could cause injury from unexpected startup or release of stored energy, with applicable conditions and exceptions for normal production; an authorized employee must have real duty training, and a title does not automatically authorize. Stored energy is eliminated, disconnected, restrained, or made safe, and isolation and de-energization are verified before work, not uniformly zero energy; a stop button is not isolation, and re-energization follows procedure with verification of equipment, personnel clearing, and notification, so an anomaly disappearing does not automatically grant re-energization authority. US 1910.212 requires appropriate machine guarding at the point of operation and at in-running and rotating parts, and hand tools cannot replace guarding; guards must not be removed or bypassed for hazardous operation on one's own, and maintenance disassembly follows the actual control procedure, and not all disassembly is treated as prohibited.
Judgment five: whether repetitive motion and awkward twisting postures are controlled

Editorial human factors check: assess force posture, repetition intensity, and duration, prioritize checking engineering improvements such as workstation and tools, and then arrange task rotation or breaks on site, escalating persistent discomfort promptly. The NIOSH general risk guidance supports assessment of repetition, force, posture, and duration, intensity, and frequency, and is not an incidence rate or personal diagnosis for this occupation. Engineering elimination, substitution, and tool and workstation changes come first, with management controls such as rotation and rest as a supplement, and PPE cannot replace more effective measures; the specific plan is determined by the actual assessment, and no uniform break duration is given.
Judgment six: whether production and test records are traceable
Write the work order number, material batch, winding parameters, test results, anomaly handling, and time clearly so that others can review under what conditions this coil was wound and tested.

paragraphs: The six directions share electrical and mechanical common sense, fine operation, working to documents, and quality record habits. The main difference is the object: repairers handle fault repair, aviation assembly handles aviation parts using the corresponding process documents, electrical and electronic assembly covers many kinds of parts, machine assembly leans toward complete units, timing devices deal with precision mechanisms, and feeding and offbearing focus on material flow; this occupation mainly forms and finishes coils. There is no same-basis evidence to rank these directions by document strictness or level of responsibility.

The comparison basis is the public tasks, work objects, and outputs of this occupation and the listed adjacent occupations; the fixed occupation links are used for locating, and the comparison is an editorial compilation and does not constitute authorization or mutual recognition of qualifications.

The table below compares positions and occupations adjacent to this occupation: motor and power tool repairers, aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers, electrical and electronic equipment assemblers, engine and other machine assemblers, timing device assemblers and adjusters, and machine feeders and offbearers. The four columns respectively answer the same kinds of questions: what this direction does, where the key difference from this occupation lies, and what kind of person is better suited to choose it.

Motor and power tool repairers focus on fault diagnosis and repair, with damaged or to-be-maintained motors and tools as their object; this occupation centers on winding wire into qualified coils to specification and documenting the electrical test results.
People willing to do troubleshooting and repair suit that direction; people willing to wind steadily to specification and check piece by piece suit this occupation.
Mainly fault diagnosis, repair, and trial run records.
Motor and power tool repairers

Aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assembly centers on assembling and aligning aviation structures and control systems, using the corresponding dimensional, torque, and traceability documents; this occupation centers on coil forming, end and insulation treatment, and inspection. Different product requirements cannot be used to rank them high or low.
People willing to work to strict documents in an aviation assembly environment suit that direction; people willing to do coil winding and electrical testing suit this occupation.
Mainly aviation assembly and inspection and traceability documents.
Aircraft structure, surfaces, rigging, and systems assemblers

Electrical and electronic equipment assemblers cover a broader range of component assembly, wiring, and complete-unit connection; this occupation's output centers on the finished wound coil and its electrical test results, with a relatively focused process.
People willing to do multi-process component assembly and wiring suit that direction; people willing to go deep and precise around a single process suit this occupation.
Mainly component assembly and wiring and complete-unit test records.
Electrical and electronic equipment assemblers

Engine and other machine assemblers lean more toward complete-machine mechanical and electrical combination and final assembly; this occupation centers on coil forming and finishing as an upstream process.
People willing to do complete-unit assembly and final assembly debugging suit that direction; people willing to do upstream precision winding suit this occupation.
Mainly complete-unit assembly and final assembly test records.
Engine and other machine assemblers

Timing device assemblers and adjusters focus on assembling and timekeeping adjustment of precision timing devices, with high demands on tiny tolerances and feel; this occupation centers on winding, electrical performance, and insulation treatment, and its output is not timekeeping accuracy.
People willing to do tiny-part assembly and adjustment suit that direction; people willing to do winding and electrical testing suit this occupation.
Mainly assembly and adjustment and timekeeping inspection records.
Timing device assemblers and adjusters

Feeding and offbearing centers on supplying equipment with material, removing finished products, and handling; whether winding parameters and electrical performance belong to a given position is still checked against the actual duties and authorization.

People willing to do production line feeding, handling, and machine watching suit that direction; people willing to take responsibility for winding parameters and electrical testing suit this occupation.
Mainly feeding and output and handover records.
Machine feeders and offbearers

Editorial transfer suggestions: repair adds fault diagnosis and trial runs, aviation assembly adds product documents and torque inspection, electrical and electronic assembly adds wiring and multi-part assembly, complete-unit assembly adds final assembly debugging, timing devices add assembly and timekeeping adjustment, and feeding and offbearing adds material pacing. Fine operation and record habits are transferable, but applicable training, qualifications, and position authorization must be checked separately, mutual recognition of existing qualifications is not guaranteed, and re-certification is not uniformly required.

Direct answer: the risks this occupation most needs to judge in advance come from four places — winding parameters, wire gauge, and turns deviating from specification causing batch electrical non-conformance, end stripping, bending, and insulation insertion being unsound causing insulation or continuity defects, serious injury from rotating parts catching and from unexpected startup during jam clearing and maintenance, and cumulative human factors injury from highly repetitive wrist motion and awkward twisting postures; runaway electrical test determinations and untraceable records are also long-term problems.

values: Paper materials

Task: on paper only, review the three coil samples A/B/C for W-07-v2 and record the reasons for pending release, without connecting power or running equipment. Fictional specification: wire M2, insulation sheet I2, 99—101 turns, tension setting T2, end 4—6 millimeters, and no crossed wire layers. A: M2/I2, 100 turns, T2, end 5 millimeters, no crossing, continuity pass. B: old M1/I1, 102 turns, T1, end 5 millimeters, crossing, continuity fail. C: M2, insulation batch number missing, 100 turns, T2, end 7 millimeters, no crossing, continuity pass. All are grading materials, not actual process parameters.

Given exercise control: work order v1 is void; all samples may apply for release only when the material batch, first-article confirmer, and authorized inspection signature are complete. A has a complete batch but lacks both the first-article and inspection signatures; B has complete records but does not meet process; C lacks the insulation batch and the inspection signature. Given event E-01: the guard is bypassed and the isolation verification is not recorded, and the supervisor authorization box is empty. The reference handling can only be stopping the work plan in the exercise, marking it pending authorization, and escalating; write no real lockout steps.

Fictional boundary: you may only read the table and make marks, and may not touch any equipment. Real protective equipment and workstation arrangements are determined by the on-site hazard assessment; the materials give no hazard assessment or applicable test procedure, which must be listed as to be obtained. The end and turn thresholds are only grading inputs for this exercise and cannot be transferred to real processes.
Checking and handling

Check the material, 99—101 turns, T2, end 4—6 millimeters, and no crossing item by item against v2; separate specification mismatches from missing traceability. Write the determination and the evidence location for A/B/C, keeping all pending release; report defects to the authorized quality person and supplement evidence for missing records, and do not rework, retest, or sign on your own.

Step three: record E-01 and the missing supervisor authorization and isolation verification, propose stopping the work plan, and escalate to the equipment and safety authorizer. description.text: Coil winders, tapers, and finishers operate or tend winding machines to wind coils for electrical components and equipment such as resistors, transformers, and motors, centered on end and insulation treatment, electrical testing, and equipment tending: the tasks and work context, the US wage and employment basis shown on the O*NET page (the exact 51-2021.00 basis is labeled), the mainland China industry average proxy and occupational-level gap, entry and qualification paths, and risks and one practice run, all in one view.

subject.summary: Operate or tend winding machines to wind wire into coils used in electrical components (such as resistors and transformers) and in electrical equipment and instruments (such as field cores, forms, armature cores, motors, generators, and control devices): determine the material and part types from the work order and specification, select and load workpieces and materials, use hand tools to terminate, reconnect, and trim wire and insulation, cut, strip, and bend the wire ends at the coil ends, use sheet insulation to line the slots and insert the coils, apply solution or varnish to the wound parts and bake them, use measuring devices to inspect and test wound electrical parts and record the test results, disassemble and assemble motors and repair and maintain electrical parts and machine parts, and record production and operating data on the required forms.
